title: Stack That Pops the Most Common
statement:
Build a stack-like container whose pop does not return the top item. It returns the value that occurs most often among the items currently inside.

  • FreqStack() creates an empty container.
  • push(val) adds one copy of val.
  • pop() removes and returns one copy of the most frequent value. If several values share the highest count, take the one whose latest copy was pushed most recently, that is, the one nearest the top.

pop is never called on an empty container. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the container, and the expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.out: [null, null, null, null, null, null, null, 4, 7, 4, 9, 7, 4]
examples.why: 4 appears three times, so it goes first. Then 4 and 7 both appear twice; the 7 sitting at position 4 is nearer the top than any 4, so 7 wins the tie.
After the first 5 leaves, 3 has the higher count. After that both have count 1 and the remaining 3 is on top, so 3 comes out twice in a row.

constraints: At most 200 000 calls to push and pop
pop is only called when the container is not empty
hints: Keep a count per value. Knowing the highest count is easy, but how do you know which value with that count is nearest the top?
Imagine one separate stack per count level: the first copy of a value goes onto stack 1, its second copy onto stack 2, and so on. What does the top of the highest stack hold?

pop takes from the stack for the current maximum count, decrements that value's count, and lowers the maximum when that stack becomes empty. Each value's earlier copies are still waiting on the lower stacks.

explain.intuition:
Split the pushes into layers. The first copy of each value lands on layer 1, the second copy on layer 2, and so on, and each layer is an ordinary stack. The highest non-empty layer holds exactly the values with the highest count, and its top is the one pushed most recently. That is precisely the item pop must return.

Popping it lowers that value's count by one, and its earlier copies are already sitting on the lower layers in the right order. So no searching or re-sorting is ever needed: every operation touches one hash map entry and one stack top.
steps: Keep count: value → how many copies are inside, layers: count level → stack of values, and top: the highest level in use.
push(val): increment count[val] to c, push val onto layers[c], and raise top to c if needed.
If layers[top] is now empty, decrease top by one. Return val.
pitfalls: Using a heap keyed only by count. Ties must go to the most recent push, so the key also needs a push timestamp.
Moving a value from layer c to layer c + 1 on push instead of adding a new copy. Its copy on layer c must stay, so it can be popped again later at count c.
Lowering top by more than one. Because counts change one at a time, the next layer down is never empty when the top one runs out.

solutions.title: Scan the whole stack on pop
solutions.idea: Keep a plain array and the counts. On pop, find the highest count, then scan from the top for the first value that has it.

solutions.title: One stack per count level
solutions.idea: The k-th copy of a value goes onto stack k. The top of the highest non-empty stack is always the answer.

followups: Solve it with a heap ordered by (count, push time). What does it cost per operation compared to the layered stacks?
Add a peek() that returns the value pop would return without removing it.
